content:
Every December two claims meet. One says that 25 December is the birthday of Jesus (peace be upon him). The other, repeated by Christians and Muslims alike, says that the Church took a pagan festival, the birthday of the Unconquered Sun, and renamed it Christmas.

Both claims say more than the evidence does. The Gospels give no date, the early Christians proposed several, and the historians who have studied the question most closely do not agree on how 25 December was chosen.

This article aims to provide context to the question, insha'Allah, in six facts from the Gospels, the early Christian writers and the scholarship on the date. The Quran speaks of the birth and gives no date either: "So peace is on me the day I was born, the day that I die, and the day that I shall be raised up to life (again)!" (19:33).[1]

Only Matthew and Luke tell of the birth. Matthew places it "in the days of King Herod" (Matthew 2:1). Luke ties it to a decree "from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled", the first "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" (Luke 2:1 to 2).[2] Neither names a month or a day.

Luke's shepherds were "staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock" (Luke 2:8).[2] Writers have read this as proof of spring or autumn, and of winter too. The verse names no season, and it cannot carry a date.

The Quran tells the birth in Surah Maryam and gives no date. Its "fresh ripe dates" (19:25) are God's provision for Mary, and the Quran has already said that God provided for her "without measure" (3:37).[1] They do not fix a month.

Around the year 200, Clement of Alexandria recorded the calculations of his day. "And there are those who have determined not only the year of our Lord's birth, but also the day; and they say that it took place in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus, and in the twenty-fifth day of Pachon."[3]

Pachon is a month of the Egyptian calendar, and its twenty-fifth day falls on 20 May. Clement goes on: "Further, others say that He was born on the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth of Pharmuthi", which is 19 or 20 April.[3] He does not mention 25 December.

These Christians cared about the date and did not know it. They worked it out, and they reached different answers.

The first clear record of 25 December comes from Rome. A calendar compiled in 354, known as the Chronography of 354, lists the commemorations of the martyrs, and its first entry reads: "VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae", "the eighth day before the kalends of January: Christ born in Bethlehem of Judea".[4]

The eighth day before the kalends of January is 25 December. The calendar gathers older lists, so the feast may be older than 354. What the calendar proves is a Roman feast on that day by the middle of the fourth century.

Popular writing says the Church chose 25 December to replace the birthday of Sol Invictus. Historians call this the History of Religions Theory. Its rival, the Calculation Theory, holds that Christians dated the conception of Jesus to 25 March, the date they also gave to his death, and counted nine months forward.[5]

C. Philipp E. Nothaft, reviewing the research in Church History, finds that each theory explains part of the evidence and meets real objections. He asks for "a more nuanced approach to the history of Christmas", one that allows for influence between religions and takes early Christian chronology seriously.[5]

Paul Bradshaw, in The Oxford Handbook of Christmas, also weighs both theories without declaring a winner.[6] The claim that the Church knowingly copied one pagan holiday is stronger than the evidence. So is the claim that the Roman festival world played no part at all.

Rome's date was not the only one. Bradshaw begins his account with an Egyptian festival: "The origins of Christmas lie in an Egyptian festival on 6 January." That feast, the Epiphany or Theophany, celebrated the birth of Jesus, and in many places his baptism as well.[6]

The Roman date travelled east slowly. Robert Edwards traces it to Constantinople under the emperor Theodosius I, from his arrival in the city in 380, and from there to Cappadocia, Pontus and Antioch, carried by travelling clergy.[7] Gregory of Nazianzus preached his sermon "On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ" in Constantinople in that period. It opens: "Christ is born, glorify Him."[8]

Some Orthodox churches now keep Christmas on 7 January. They keep 25 December by the Julian calendar, which today falls on 7 January in the Gregorian; they do not claim a different birthday. The Armenian Apostolic Church still keeps the Nativity and the Theophany together on 6 January.

The evidence supports a modest conclusion. 25 December is an ancient Christian feast, attested in Rome by 354, and it was never a recorded birthday. Historians can trace when the feast appears and how it spread, and none of them can recover the day Jesus was born.

For Muslims this costs nothing. The Quran directs attention to the meaning of the birth, and gives it in the child's own words: "I am indeed a servant of Allah: He hath given me revelation and made me a prophet" (19:30).[1] We set out what the Quran says of him in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God.

The bottom line

Matthew and Luke give no date for the birth of Jesus, and the Christians of Clement's day calculated dates in April and May. Rome kept 25 December by 354, the East kept 6 January, and the Roman date reached Constantinople around 380. Historians still debate whether a calculation from 25 March or the festivals of Rome led to the choice.

Neither slogan survives the evidence. "The Bible gives 25 December" is false, and "Christmas is a renamed pagan festival" claims a certainty the historians do not have. The Quran asks nothing of the date and gives the meaning: "Verily Allah is my Lord and your Lord: Him therefore serve ye" (19:36).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 3:37; 19:16 to 36, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:1 to 20 (World English Bible).
  3. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata I.21, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2.
  4. Chronography of 354, part 12, "Depositio Martyrum", in Theodor Mommsen, ed., Chronica Minora I (Berlin, 1892), pp. 71–72.
  5. C. Philipp E. Nothaft, "The Origins of the Christmas Date: Some Recent Trends in Historical Research", Church History 81, no. 4 (2012), pp. 903–911, doi:10.1017/S0009640712001941.
  6. Paul F. Bradshaw, "The Dating of Christmas: The Early Church", in Timothy Larsen, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Christmas (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020), doi:10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198831464.013.2.
  7. Robert G. T. Edwards, "Travelling Festivals in Late Antiquity: How Christmas Came to the Greek East", Journal of Ecclesiastical History 75, no. 3 (2024), pp. 427–443, doi:10.1017/S002204692300009X.
  8. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 38, "On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ", in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 7.
